source.title: RegMix: Data Mixture as Regression for Language Model Pre-training
source.authors: Qian Liu; Xiaosen Zheng; Niklas Muennighoff; Guang-Tao Zeng; Long-Xu Dou; Tianyu Pang; Jing Jiang; Min Lin

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures relationships between validation loss and downstream performance, using data-mixture variation rather than the original parameter/token/compute scaling-law fits. It also tests whether data-mixture rankings transfer across model sizes and token quantities.
record.gate_note: The paper reports prediction of data-mixture rankings and loss-to-downstream correlations, but does not run a conventional parameter, token, or compute scaling-law sweep or identify a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Downstream benchmark comparisons between RegMix and other mixture-selection methods are not rows unless they measure the claim’s loss-to-performance or scale-predictability relationship.
record.test_reason: The study is not an original source. Its own 64×1B runs correlate validation loss with 13 downstream tasks across data mixtures. Its 7B runs track downstream accuracy as training tokens grow. Both bear on V6 in a new setting: variation comes from data mixture, not model scale. It runs no parameter, token or compute power-law fit, no allocation sweep and no shape comparison, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but too narrow. The main conclusion is that RegMix, a regression over small-proxy runs, finds high-performing mixtures that transfer to 1B and 7B models, resting on rank invariance. The authors also conclude that data mixture strongly affects downstream performance, and that web-corpus (Pile-CC) loss correlates best with downstream tasks. They add that domain interactions are complex and that mixture effects are not captured by simple per-domain scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses regression over data-mixture weights and validation outcomes, not the original parameter/token/compute power-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Regression method changes prediction results: LightGBM has higher reported rank correlations than linear regression in the tested settings. Proxy-model count and proxy training-token count also affect regression performance (Figure 4).

fits_no_version.finding: Regression on 512 1M-parameter proxy runs predicts mixture rankings for 60M and 1B models (ρ up to 97.12). Mixture rankings stay stable from 1M to 1B parameters (Figure 15 ρ≈0.94–0.99).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relative ranking of pretraining data mixtures is invariant across model and token scales.

fits_no_version.finding: Log loss versus log domain weight is near-linear for DM Mathematics but complex for Pile-CC and most other domains.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Per-domain data-mixture scaling laws in a domain's own weight hold only for some domains.

record.problems: The central scaling-law claim is not directly tested: there are no power-law fits in parameter count, tokens, or compute, and no compute-optimal allocation analysis. The reported cross-scale regression results concern mixture rankings rather than power-law loss extrapolation. Some relevant correlations are qualitative in the text or plotted, and the rank-invariance experiments extend only to 1B parameters.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported downstream benchmark comparisons among mixture-selection methods were extracted where they measured only method performance rather than loss-to-downstream predictability or a scaling-law relation.

untested.parts: No fit of held-out loss against parameters, tokens or compute.
No power-law extrapolation of loss. The cross-scale prediction is regression on mixture rankings.
No compute-optimal allocation analysis. The 1B/25B budget is simply set Chinchilla-optimal.
No fitted functional form linking loss or scale to downstream accuracy, and no prediction of larger-model accuracy from smaller ones. MMLU and GSM8K are excluded as near-random.
No comparison of fitted exponents or of fitting choices.

missing.what: Downstream accuracy of 7B RegMix and Human models at 25B, 50B, 75B and 100B tokens on 13 tasks. The authors say most tasks show positive scaling, except tasks like MultiRC. Figure-only.
Per-task correlation coefficients between each Pile domain's validation loss and each downstream task. Tasks such as Social IQA, LogiQA and MultiRC may show weak correlation; heatmap only.

record.verdict_notes: The loss–downstream evidence comes from variation across data mixtures at fixed scale (1B/25B), not across scale. This makes it indirect evidence for V6's 'with pretraining loss' clause. Most supporting values are qualitative or heatmap-only.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss against parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
The paper predicts data-mixture performance or ranking with regression, not losses using power laws fitted on smaller runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation sweep or fitted allocation exponents.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The experiments concern text pre-training and do not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

Tests loss-to-downstream correlations across data mixtures and reports downstream performance over training-token quantities, but does not establish a general predictive function of pretraining loss or scale across models and tasks.
It examines loss against domain-mixture weights, not the dependence of standard scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting and training setup.

rows.operation_detail: Compare validation-loss rankings across model sizes and token scales
rows.measure: Cross-scale correlation of data-mixture validation-loss rankings
rows.value: High rank correlation coefficients across all model and token scales; individual values are shown in Figure 15
rows.note: This tests rank invariance of mixtures, not power-law prediction of loss.

rows.measure: Correlation coefficient between validation loss and downstream performance
rows.note: The authors take the negative of validation loss when calculating the correlation.

rows.subject: 64× 1B models
rows.operation_detail: Compare validation-loss correlations with downstream benchmark performance across training domains
rows.value: Pile-CC validation loss shows the strongest correlation with most downstream tasks
rows.note: The paper describes the pattern across most tasks but does not give the full set of correlation coefficients in the text.
rows.check: This is a relative comparison across validation domains, given without coefficients. It shows that loss–downstream predictability depends on which validation loss is used: Pile-CC beats Wikipedia, contrary to the authors' expectation.

rows.subject: C4100Domain validation domains
rows.operation_detail: Correlate validation losses on URL domains with downstream task performance
rows.value: More than 85% of the domains exhibit a very strong correlation with Pile-CC
rows.note: The text says the www.ign.com domain closely mirrors the Pile-CC correlation graph.
rows.check: Subject is the 64×1B models evaluated on C4100Domain URL-domain losses, not the validation domains themselves. The value compares each domain's correlation pattern with Pile-CC's pattern.

rows.subject: RegMix and Human 7B models

rows.value: figure only; authors state that RegMix and Human struggle to improve on MultiRC even with increased token amounts

rows.check: Figure-only. The 7B models run 25B–100B tokens. The authors say both mixtures struggle to improve on MultiRC (Table 10: 52.6 and 51.0 at 100B).

relationships.condition: 64×1B models (25B tokens) across data mixtures, using Pile-CC or web-domain validation loss
relationships.reason: HellaSwag correlation with negated Pile-CC loss is 'remarkably close to 1.0'. Pile-CC correlates most strongly with most tasks, and over 85% of C4 URL domains show a similar pattern (r14, r15, r16).
relationships.display_finding: HellaSwag correlation with negated Pile-CC loss approached 1.0, Pile-CC was most strongly associated with most tasks, and over 85% of C4 URL domains showed similar patterns.

relationships.reason: Loss–downstream correlation is strongest for web loss and weaker for other Pile domains such as Wikipedia. Predictability therefore depends on which loss is used (r15; coefficients shown only in Figure 5).
relationships.display_finding: Web validation loss correlated most strongly with downstream performance, while losses on other Pile domains, including Wikipedia, correlated less strongly.

relationships.condition: MultiRC on 7B models from 25B to 100B tokens
relationships.reason: The authors say both mixtures struggle to improve on MultiRC with more tokens, calling it a task that may not follow scaling laws (r17).
relationships.display_finding: Both data mixtures struggled to improve MultiRC as training increased from 25B to 100B tokens in 7B models.
